content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes DMLP, a label purifier for learning from noisy labels using a bilevel optimization framework.
The key idea is to decouple learning of feature extraction and classification by a linear layer.
As a feature extractor, off-the-shelf self-supervised pre-trained models are used.
Since the decoupling, label purification in the classifier becomes linear regression, which has a closed-form solution and thus avoids expensive bilevel optimization over neural networks.
Empirical results show state-of-the-art results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strength

1. Decoupling learning of the feature extractor and the classifier avoids instability of training and collapse of feature learning when labels are extremely noisy. 
2. Thanks to this decoupling, training of the classifier is just a linear regression, having a closed-form solution. As a result, its meta-learning part becomes simple and avoids the complex unrolling-iteration scheme like MAML. 
3. The proposed method is simple and can be combined with other methods for LNL.

# Weakness

1. The experimental settings are unrealistic and depend on a strong assumption that enough amount of cleanly labeled data is available for meta learning. On CIFARs, they used 1000 samples. Practically, we need additional cleanly labeled data for model selection.
2. Strength 1overlaps with, e.h., Sato et al. 2019 "Breaking inter-layer co-adaptation by classifier anonymization" and Sato et al. 2021 "Breaking inter-layer co-adaptation by classifier anonymization".
3. Strength 2 overlaps with, e.g., Bamos 2019 "Differentiable Optimization-Based Modeling for Machine Learning".
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:

The training protocols of feature extractors were unclear, such as the datasets that were used.

# Quality

* The mathematical notations are confusing and have rooms to improve.
For example, $p$ is initially used to represent prediction results (sec 3.1), and later it is used as an index (eq 9).

# Novelty

As discussed in Strength and Weaknesses, the novelty seems to be limited and overlaps with not-cited existing works.

# Reproducibility

The method seems to be simple and easy to implement, so I think it is not difficult to reproduce the experiments.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Zo6h
content.comment:
Q1: **The experimental settings are unrealistic and depend on a strong assumption that enough amount of cleanly labeled data is available for meta learning.**

- We kindly argue that the small set of clean validation samples has been widely adopted by meta label correction methods for noisy label learning [4-7,11]. And it is practical and feasible to collect such a small clean set, e.g., we demonstrate that with only ~0.1% of training data as the validation set, DMLP can obtain high accuracy (>75.5%) on real-world noisy Clothing1M dataset.  



Q2: **Strength 1 overlaps with [2].**

- To the best of our knowledge, [2] belongs to a family of network randomization methods, which aims to improve the generalization of deep models by using randomly generated, weak classifiers during the backbone training. However, DMLP is designed as a meta label purifier for LNL problem, which decouples the meta-learning objective into the backbone and label distribution learning to facilitate accurate label correction.


Q3: **Strength 2 overlaps with [3].**

- We kindly argue that in this work, we make empirically observation that the coupled optimization objective within traditional meta label correction methods is sub-optimal in the context of noisy labels, as far as we know, this is not been studied before in the field of LNL. And motivated by this, we first propose the decouped label corrector to tackle with this problem. We believed that the proposed method has potential to inspire more works that rethinking the meta label correction paradigm.


Q4: **The training protocols of feature extractors were unclear, such as the datasets that were used.**

- The training protocols of feature extractors are shown in the experimental details part of Appendix A.3. Specifically, for fair comparisons, we don't use extra datasets for self-supervised training. For example, for the training on the CIFAR10/100, only the data in the CIFAR10/100 is involved in the self-supervised training of our feature extractors. 


Q5: **The mathematical notations are confusing and have rooms to improve. For example, p is initially used to represent prediction results (sec 3.1), and later it is used as an index (eq 9).**

- Thanks for your advice. We have corrected this issue to make the mathematical notations clear. Please refer to the revised manuscript for more details.

content.title: Response to Reviewer USBq
content.comment:
Q1: **A comparison with self-supervised representation + MLC or MSLC is needed.**

- **Please be responsible and carefully read the paper till the end.** We emphasize that the comparison between DMLP and MLC (MSLC) + self-supervised pretrained weights is shown in Table.6 (more results can also be found in Table.10). All the results indicate that DMLP is superior to the coupled (MLC. MSLC) baseline competitors.


Q2: **C2D + DivideMix can easily beat DMLP-Naive, and sometimes beat DMLP-DivideMix in Table 2.**

- **Please be responsible and do not propose WRONG conclusion.** C2D is compared on CIFAR-10/100 both with symmetric (Table.1) and asymmetric (Table.2) noise, also real-world noisy datasets Clothing1M (Table.3). Note that DMLP-DivdeMix achieves consistently **better results** than C2D. 
- Also, directly compare C2D-DivideMix with DMLP-Naive is not totally fair since the former adopt a strong LNL method and the latter only adopts simple cross-entropy, in spite of this, DMLP-Naive beats C2D-Naive in some case of CIFAR-100 and Clothing1M of real noise.

Q3: **The algorithm idea is similar to REED, containing three stages.**

- We clarify that the proposed DMLP is a meta-label purifier, which is built on the empirical observation that coupled optimization over label and model weight can not achieve an optimal routine. This is different from REED, which resorts to decoupling the backbone and linear classifier for more separable sample selection and semi-supervised retraining over full model on the selected sample sets (clean and un-labeled). 


Q4: **Figure 3 is not clear, e.g., EMA update in Figure 3(a) is not mentioned in the main paper, and what’s the meaning of the F(·;θ)  in the Figure 3(b)?**

- EMA update is formulated in Eq.(9). F(·;θ) denotes the parameters in existing LNL methods that DMLP can work with.



Q5: **If DMLP does not use the third stage, what about the results?**

- The results of DMLP without the re-training strategy (i.e., EAC as classifier) are shown in Sec.A.3.5, Table.11.


Q6: **The "Intrinsic Primary Correction" is similar to [1]**
- [1] is proposed to handle the few-shot learning problem, which is different from the noisy label learning context. Moreover, the meta-parameters to optimize in [2] involve backbone training. On the contrary, the proposed IPC explicitly decoupled the backbone training from meta objective into self-supervised pretraining, and keep fixed during the label correction process.


Q7: **The additional clean samples are not reasonable. It is better to present the result of DMLP that does not use the validation set in Table 3**
- We kindly argue that the small set of clean validation samples has been widely adopted by meta label correction methods for noisy label learning [4-7,11]. And it is practical and feasible to collect such a small clean set, e.g., we demonstrate that with only ~0.1% of training data as the validation set, DMLP can obtain high accuracy (>75.5%) on real-world noisy Clothing1M dataset.  

Q8: **How to apply the DMLP into the existing LNL framework?**
- Please carefully read the method part. The application of DMLP is elaborated in Sec.3.3. Specifically, the purifier labels generated by our DMLP can be directly applied in the existing LNL framework as training samples to boost their performance. 

Q9: **Semi-supervised learning only runs CIFAR-10.**
- The results on CIFAR-100 are also shown in the table below, where our DMLP can consistently outperform these methods as well:

|  Dataset |CIFAR100 |   |   | | |
|--|:-------:|:------:|:------:|:-------:|:-------:|
Method                    | MeanTeacher | MixMatch  |FixMatch  | UDA  | DMLP |
| Acc |31.0   | 57.7 | 56.3  |  56.1 |  60.1 |

replying_to: Replying to The concerns are not perfectly clarified

content.title: Response to reviewer USBq
content.comment:
The extra questions are responsed as follow:

Q1: **Not totally fair to compared with methods without using such validation set.**

A1: We have compared not only with methods that do not use validation set, but also with many methods that use the same validation set with us. The results were shown in Table1/2/3. It shows that we have a significant advantage over all these methods under a fair experimental setting. 

Q2: **DMLP-DivideMix has substantially more algorithm steps (IPC,EAC) than C2D-DivideMix, as well as additional validation set, while only brings subtle improvements.**

A2: We emphasize that DMLP is computationally efficient in terms of time cost for label correction, since it only involves a few trainable parameters (i.e., IPC and EAC). Specifically, it takes only 15 minutes to refine the label of the CIFAR10/100. And for the training of C2D-DivideMix, it needs 360 epochs while for fair comparison with most of methods, DMLP-DivideMix is only trained for 300 epochs. However, DMLP-DivideMix can still perform much better than C2D-Dividemix across all the settings. Therefore, our DMLP-DivideMix needs less time for training and shows greater advantage over C2D-DivideMix. Finally, it is notable that compared to C2D-Dividemix, our method shows a very clear advantage in high noise case (e.g. 7.1% improvement in 90% noisy case on CIFAR-100) and real-world noisy dataset Clothing1M (e.g. around 4% improvement). So it is **NOT** a subtle improvements as you claimed.

Q3: **The result of Semi-supervised learning is not convinced. Fixmatch achieves 94.93 point with 250 labels, while achieves 88.1 point in Table 8 on CIFAR-10.**

A3: The result of 94.93% in the FixMatch paper is produced using Wide ResNet-28 trained for 1024 epochs. Besides, the validation set in the manuscript of FixMatch is constructed by uniformly selecting the same number of samples from each class, while in our DMLP, the validation set is constructed by uniformly sampling from the whole dataset without considering the sample number for each class, which is more pratical in real-world applications. Therefore, for fair comparison, we retrain its official code with our settings, where FixMatch is trained with the same validation set as ours for 300 epochs with ResNet-18, which has much less parameters than Wide ResNet-28. As a result, the Fixmatch achieves 88.1 accuracy.

Q4: **Meta Pseudo Labels also use meta-learning to correct the wrong labels in semi-supervised learning, I think it is necessary to compared with it.**

A4: It should be noted that our method is designed for noise-label learning rather than for semi-supervised methods. The semi-supervised experiments are only conducted as a plus to further highlight the potential advantages of our method, which was not studied in any of the previous noisy learning methods using validation sets to the best of our knowledge. Therefore we do not agree that the comparision with more semi-supervised techniques are necessary as we focus on learning with noisy labels in this work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers the problem of training deep neural networks under label noise. The authors argue that state-of-the-art meta-learning methods do not perform well empirically due to their bilevel optimization formulation which limits representation ability and accuracy of corrected labels. To remedy this, the authors propose a decoupled approach, DMLP, that decouples the label correction process into label-free representation learning and label purification conducted in two distinct phases.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths
* Learning with noisy labels is a topic of high importance and interest to the wider ML community.
* The proposed method is novel compared to prior approaches that have predominantly focused on bilevel optimization formulations to solve the problem of learning with noisy labels.
* Empirical evaluations are provided that demonstrate the improved performance of the method when combined with prior approaches.

## Weaknesses
* The feature descriptors are assumed to be representative enough that a linear regression problem can be used in conjunction with the obtained representations to compute the output label. Isn’t this process the same as neural network training, where the penultimate layer’s outputs can be interpreted as the representation and the last layer essentially solves the linear regression problem given these representations? It’s not clear to me what the benefit of this decoupling is mathematically.
* The description of the method is very dense and certain components of the method seem arbitrary and not well justified. For example, why is an entropy term added to the linear regression problem in Eq. 6? Why is there no regularization term $\lambda$ associated with this regularization? In Eq. 7, the solution is computed iteratively using gradient descent, and then at the very end, a softmax function is applied to the unconstrained solution to get probabilities (a label vector). This is not a proper implementation of projected gradient descent, which I gather is what the authors want to do here. The projection to the probability simplex should be done at each iteration of the gradient descent algorithm after the gradient update. In Eq. 8, an entropy function is once again added with no regularization term and it is not clear why. In Eq. 9, a momentum term is applied, which introduces even further hyperparameters that need to be tuned. Overall, it is not clear what the benefit of having two components, IPC and EAC, is. Empirical evaluations with only a single component activated would go a long way in justifying the need for both components simultaneously.
* Mathematically, it seems that the bilevel optimization formulation captures the interdependencies in the problem more accurately. In light of this, what explains their poor empirical performance as the authors claim? This is not made clear in the paper.
* If the proposed method can generate clean labels more accurately than prior methods, than why is the method by itself (DMLP-Naive) not enough to outperform competing approaches? In other words, why are combinations of the method with other methods (e.g., DivideMix) needed? Moreover, it is not clear to me whether this is a fair comparison, as other methods could also be mixed-and-matched to obtain further improvements in performance.
* There is no information regarding the number of trials that the results were averaged over and no standard deviation figures are included for the results in Sec. 4.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Please see the section above for comments regarding clarity, quality, novelty, and reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper addresses a problem that is highly relevant to the ML community and challenges the paradigm of most existing approaches that use a bilevel optimization framework. The authors propose an interesting idea that hinges on a decoupled approach to label correction. However, the exposition of the approach is dense and certain components of the method are not well-motivated or justified in a principled way. It also seems that the method only achieves the state-of-the-art results when combined with existing LNL approaches, and it is not clear why this combination is needed and whether this results in a fair comparison to prior work. In light of these considerations, I lean towards rejection.

content.title: Response to Reviewer TiU1
content.comment:
Q1: **It’s not clear what the benefit of this decoupling is mathematically?**

- As discussed in Sec3.1, Eq.(1) and Eq.(2) depict the two different objective functions between typical meta label corrector and DMLP. Specifically, DMLP fixes the feature extractor ${\theta_G}$, and then obtains the closed-form solution $w^*(Y_t)$, so that we can focus on correcting the labels (Eq.(6)) more efficiently. While typical meta learning methods involve a coupled optimization over model weights and labels, which we empirically verified is sub-optimal to our proposition.


Q2: **The description of the method is very dense and certain components of the method seem arbitrary and not well justified, e.g., why add an entropy term, why there is no regularization term, why need IPC and EAC?**

We claim that each component in the method part is added on specific purpose:

- The entropy term is added in Eq.(6) and Eq.(8) as  regularization to sharpen the predicted label distribution, this is similar to PENCIL[8]. 
- In pratice, we add a small unit diagonal matrix in Eq.(5) to ensure the solution matrix is invertible, this is equivalent to an L2-regularization term to Eq.(4).
- The usage of softmax: since our goal is to regeress a normalized categorical distribution, we transform the opitizable variable to a series of unormalized logit value $y$, then for each iteration, the regression goal is $y'=softmax(y)$, and the backpropagated gradient can be $\partial L/\partial y' \cdot \partial y'/\partial y$. **This is only a way of relaxation instead of so-called gradient projection.**
- EAC aims to accelerate the purification process by looking ahead (i.e., training with) the updated labels from IPC, which reversely facilitates the label correction of IPC by providing cleaner training labels. IPC and EAC form a positive loop and mutually improve performance.
**As you said by yourself, "Empirical evaluations with only a single component activated would go a long way in justifying the need for both components simultaneously", we already provide the investigation in Table 5 if you read the paper carefully.**



Q3: **What explains the bi-level optimization formulation poor empirical performance as the authors claim?**

- You ignore the effect of noisy labels. We emphasize that in the context of LNL, the backbone is vulnerable to noisy labels, therefore such bi-level optimization indicating update backbone with noisy gradient, hindering representation ability (and reversely this will affect the quality of corrected labels). 



Q4: **The label correction accuracy of DMLP and Why are combinations of the method with other methods (e.g., DivideMix) needed?**

- Please note we claim our method focus on better label correction for downstream LNL tasks, and we verify that DMLP is able to generate more accurate labels than previous label correctors (e.g., MLC and MSLC) in Fig.6. And since DMLP can yield more clean labels, it is natural to leverage the corrected labels to boost existing LNL frameworks. DMLP-Naive can beat most competitors, this means once the label gets corrected, then a simple cross-entropy loss can obtain good results without too much complex design for data selection or reweighting. A combination with LNL of other methods can also obtain consistent performance gain. A similar comparison manner can also be found in previous LNL works[9,10].


Q5: **No standard deviation figures are included for the results in Sec. 4.**
- Following the setting of previous methods [5], we list the best and last performance during the training process to show the stability of the methods. Moreover, we also calculate the averaged results over the last 10 epoches and list the corresponding standard deviation figures of our DMLP below:

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposed a novel approach for label denoising/purify. Specifically, label noise is the one of the main challenges for obtaining high training performance. However, inaccurate labels are always existed. This work observes that the label correction and the sample representation learning cannot achieve the best performance jointly.

Due to this observation, a novel decoupled meta purification strategy is proposed which  aims to achieve the accurate label correction and the representation learning / down-stream tasks simultaneously. A non-nested meta label purifier is proposed associated with classification applications are used to evaluate the performance of the proposed model. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the method.
